runs.text: Certo ferro como debrum, ou cin-

lines.note: Saruuogane names an iron reinforcing strip on a stirrup. The scan and supplied lexical index support ruu rather than OCR mu; ferro has two r's.

runs.text: ta que eſtà nas coſtas dos eſtribos de Iapão pe-

lines.note: Completes cinta and locates the strip on the backs of Japanese stirrups. The printed pe- continues as pera below.
Gives the purpose of the strip: strengthening the stirrups. This finishes the preceding entry.

runs.text: Certa erua que comem os caualos que tem

lines.note: Sasa is described as vegetation eaten by horses. The leaf comparison below identifies the intended plant form without requiring a species-level identification.
Completes the plant description with leaves like those of little canes. The row belongs to the first sasa entry.
This second sasa is a word for sake or wine, labelled as women's vocabulary. Saqe is a Japanese synonym, not an embedded Portuguese term.
Completes the printed mo-lheres, retaining the historical vowel rather than modernizing the Portuguese word for women.
Sasagani denotes spiders. The upright P. labels poetic usage and is separated from the italic definition.

runs.text: Certo comer de arroz cozido em-

lines.note: Sasajimaki is a prepared-rice food wrapped in leaves. The source's em- begins the divided Portuguese wrapping verb.
Completes em-buralhado, describing the rice wrapped in particular leaves. The historical form buralhado is retained as printed.
Sasage names a kind of bean. This plant noun is distinct from the offering verb on the next row.
Sasage is to offer or present. The gloss reads apreſẽtar, with a long s and abbreviation tilde, not OCR aprerẽtar.
Sasagemono is an offering or present, the noun corresponding to the preceding verb.

The Portuguese gives 'each deed or work.' Both Japanese components and their circumflexes are preserved, including the mixed geô/guiô spellings; no speculative kanji identification or normalized headword is inserted. The final Portuguese vowel is read a in obra.
Sasamakura is a poetic expression for travel, explained by tabi. P. is upright; pere- begins the Portuguese description of travelling abroad.
Completes peregrinando por fora, wandering or travelling away from home. It is the definition of the preceding poetic expression.
Sasamegoto is quiet conversation, marked poetic by upright P. The secrecy qualification follows below.
Adds 'and in secret,' completing the explanation of whispered or private conversation.
Sasameki is glossed first as becoming inwardly stirred or agitated. The source divides inte-riormente across rows.
Completes the inward-agitation gloss and begins mune ga sasameku, with the Japanese verb physically divided after ſa-.
Completes the Japanese example and translates it as the heart becoming disturbed. The right edge prints a hyphen in cora-, not the OCR stop.

runs.text: ção. ¶ Item, As vezes Saſamequ, ſe to-

lines.note: Completes coração, then says Saſamequ can sometimes have another meaning. The Japanese verb is embedded in Portuguese explanatory syntax and is flagged for whole-word typeface review.

runs.text: ma por falar à puridade, & manſo.

lines.note: Completes toma and gives speaking privately and softly as the additional sense. Puridade is retained rather than replaced with a modern paraphrase.

runs.text: Lugar de muita erua que ſe parece

lines.note: Sasawara denotes an area thick with the vegetation described by the following cane-leaf comparison.
Finishes the sasa-grove description by comparing the leaves with small cane leaves.
Sasawari is to be hindered or encumbered. The historical s-form is retained instead of modernizing it to sawari.
Completes the reflexive Portuguese verb and gives mono ni sasawaru, being obstructed by something.
Translates the Japanese example as being impeded by something. The abbreviation tilde remains on u in algũa.
The corresponding noun means an impediment, obstacle, or encumbrance. The last Portuguese synonym crosses the row break.
Completes em-baraço, meaning encumbrance, and finishes the preceding noun's three-synonym Portuguese definition.

Sasayaki is to speak privately or whisper. A small irregular mark above u is not securely distinguishable from damaged or stray ink; the baseline unaccented u is retained rather than assigning an unsupported accent.
Sasayakiai is whispering to one another. The carons on both principal forms are visible; puridade corrects OCR's extra a, and ẽtreſi remains joined and abbreviated.
Sasayakimawari describes going around whispering. The Portuguese purida-de is visibly split between physical rows.

runs.text: de a diuerſas peßoas, ou em diuerſas partes.

lines.note: Specifies whispering to different people or in different places. The worn vowel in peßoas is read o rather than OCR c.
Sasaye means holding back or obstructing. Mi- begins michi, 'road,' in the following example.
Completes michi wo sasayuru, to block the road. The row's first letters belong to the divided Japanese example.
Hito wo sasayuru is explained here as speaking ill of someone. Dalguẽ preserves the abbreviation, and di- begins diante below.

runs.text: ante do ſenhor, ou de quem lhe pode empecer.

lines.note: Specifies speaking before a superior or someone able to harm the person. The Portuguese verb is empecer, with visible p, not OCR emoecer.
Sasaye todome combines obstruction with stopping or detaining. The two Japanese words remain separated as in the scan.
Sasoku denotes nimble feet; the example describes someone whose footwork is effective. The long s in Saſocuga was misread as i by OCR.

runs.text: Homem ligeiro dos pees como os que

lines.note: Hito completes the Japanese example. The Portuguese describes a light-footed person and introduces comparisons below.

runs.text: na luta, ou eſgrima ſabem bem fugir com

lines.note: Illustrates nimble footwork through evasion in wrestling or fencing. The sentence continues with os pees.
Finishes the footwork explanation. The unaccented historical pees is retained beside the earlier accented Pès.
Sasoi is calling or encouraging another to come along. Both circumflexes are visible, and the Portuguese begins with a lowercase c in this impression.

runs.text: pera ir com elle, ou leuar alguem conſigo. Vt,

lines.note: Expands the invitation sense as going with someone or taking someone along. Italic Vt introduces the following Japanese example.
Hito wo sasou is inviting a person. The noun has o, not the OCR c in Fitcuo, and the verb retains its circumflex.
Sasoi yuki combines inviting with taking someone along. The final principal form is ita, with a worn t rather than OCR r; al-guem continues at the top of column 2.
Completes al-guem from the preceding column: Sasoi yuqi means to invite someone and take that person along. This is a continuation, not a new entry.

runs.text: Modo de ſoar algũa couſa, que ſe rõ

lines.note: Sassato describes a tearing or rushing sound. The final nasal abbreviation rõ continues as rompe on the next row; no terminal hyphen is supplied because none is visible here.

runs.text: pe, ou raſga como papel, peça, &c. Vt,

lines.note: Paper and cloth illustrate the tearing sound. The Japanese example begins with Sas- at the right edge; its visible hyphen and roman type are retained.
Sassato camiuo saqu means to tear paper with the stated sound. The Portuguese printing separates pa pel slightly; the supplied spacing is retained rather than silently regularized.

runs.text: eſtrondo. Item, modo de ſoarem as ondas, ou

lines.note: The explanation first completes tearing with a loud sound, then extends the same expressive word to waves or trees. Both clauses belong to Sassato.
Trees sounding in the wind introduce Matçu fuqu, the beginning of the pine-and-wind example continued below. The paragraph sign marks a new illustration, not a separate headword.

Read caje, wind, rather than the OCR cije: the second letter is severely worn, leaving a narrow right stroke and a faint lower trace. The pine context and the Portuguese O vento support a damaged a; this remains a nonblocking glyph uncertainty. The example continues Matçu fuqu from the previous row.
The wind strikes the pines and makes them sound. Pinheiros has a clear r rather than the OCR t in pinhetros; the line closes the example.
Sassocu is glossed by the Japanese synonyms Fayaxi and sumiyaca nari, fast or prompt. These are standalone synonyms, not Japanese terms embedded in Portuguese prose.
Completes mui-to and defines the preceding adjective as very quick and hurried. The beta-shaped double-s sort in apreßada is retained.
Sassocuni is the corresponding adverb, quickly and promptly. The abbreviated grammatical label reads Aduer.; the line-final de- is visible.
Completes de-preßa, in haste, from the preceding physical line. This short row must remain part of the adverb entry.
Sasu names the roof-frame members of a house. Portuguese asnas here is the building term for rafters or trusses, not the animal sense.

runs.text: Contudo, ou na realidade, o que mais

lines.note: Sasuga receives the older connective senses nevertheless, in reality, or what is more. The Japanese headword and Portuguese explanation have distinct typefaces.

Corrected Suſuga to Saſuga from the damaged but readable a and agreement with the entry. Iua qini arazareba says that someone is not stone or wood; the source's unusual hyphen after the complete Portuguese word Na is retained.

runs.text: realidade não era como rocha, ou pao inſen-

lines.note: The Portuguese interprets the example as not being an insensible rock or piece of wood. The visible split inſen- continues on the following row; pao is not modernized.
Completes inſen-ſiuel, insensible, and closes the stone-and-wood comparison. The row is real body text despite its short length.
Sasugani refers back to Sasuga with the same meaning. Idem is the entire Portuguese-side explanation; no missing gloss is inferred.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de gancho, ou forca-

lines.note: Sasumata is a hooked or forked implement. The first vowel reads a, not the OCR u in Suſumata; the Portuguese forca- continues as forcado below.

runs.text: do que particularmente ſerue na eſgrima pera

lines.note: Completes forcado and states that the implement is especially used in fighting or fencing. The purpose follows on the next physical row.

runs.text: ter mão nas Catanas, ou pera prender alguem,

lines.note: The fork is used to restrain swords or capture someone. Catanas is a Japanese-derived noun embedded inside the Portuguese explanation and is eligible for whole-word typeface review.
This separate et-cetera row closes the Sasumata definition. It is not a catchword or marginal mark.

runs.text: Certa laya de eſcopro de carpinteiro.

lines.note: Sasunomi is a kind of carpenter's chisel. The historical laya and eſcopro are retained rather than replaced by modern Portuguese spellings.
Corrected Siſurai to Saſurai, wander in exile, from the printed a and the following related entries. Both inflection vowels have upward-opening marks, retained as carons.

runs.text: mo vago ſem lugar, nem morada certa.

lines.note: Completes co-mo and describes wandering without a settled place or dwelling. The line belongs to Sasurai, not the compound that follows.
Sasurai aruqi combines wandering with walking. The printed inflection is aruita; diuer- continues as diversas on the next line.

runs.text: ſas partes como deſterrado, ou peregrino.

lines.note: The compound means going through various places as an exile or traveler. The Portuguese sense makes the relationship between the two Japanese verbs explicit.

Sasurayebito is a wandering exile or traveler, with the register label P. printed upright. Restored the second r in Deſterrado from the paired strokes in the scan; this is not a modernization of the headword.

runs.text: que anda vago por diuerſas partes.

lines.note: The relative clause specifies someone who roams through different places. It completes the noun definition above.
Sasuri means rubbing gently, here the beginning of an explanation involving a sore body part. The historical nasal abbreviation in algũa is visible.
The first sense is rubbing a painful area; a new Japanese example starts with Taqeuo, bamboo as object. The paragraph sign separates the illustration without creating a new entry.

runs.text: Tirar a caſca por cima, ou alimpar

lines.note: Taqeuo sasuru means removing the outer surface or cleaning bamboo. This second use differs from soothing a sore body part but is explicitly given under the same verb.
Completes the bamboo-cleaning explanation. The short line belongs to Sasuri and contains no additional headword.

Sat denotes a conjecture, and Sat suru means to conjecture. The final unreleased consonant is intentionally written without a following vowel; the two Portuguese noun and verb spellings are preserved.

runs.text: Couſa que deue, ou parece ſer

lines.note: Sattçuberaxij describes what ought to be or seems fitting. The double t and ç are source spelling, not errors to reduce to modern romanization.
The example concerns a fitting manner or posture. Joined the OCR's false break within Sattçuberaxij and corrected Mado to Modo from the worn round vowel; the terminal eſ- continues below.

runs.text: tar conuenientemente, & daſſento como em ſua

lines.note: Completes eſ-tar: being appropriately settled, as in one's own home. Historical daſſento and the source's long-s sequence are retained.
Completes the comparison with being at home. This final short row belongs to the example beginning Sattçuberaxij te.

This is the adverb corresponding to Sattçuberaxij. The last letter of the abbreviated label is worn; read Adu., not the OCR Ada., from its open lower form and the grammatical function. The headword's upward-opening accent is retained as ǔ.
Sata denotes discussion or rumor. The example has vye-, not the OCR vve-: the middle letter visibly descends as y, and vyeuo on the next row forms the expression about a person.
Completes Fitono vyeuo sata suru, to talk or discuss someone. The hyphen on the previous row separates the noun from its object particle only because of physical lineation.

runs.text: Satauo caguitta coto. l, ſatano ca-

lines.note: Two related expressions describe something beyond ordinary discussion or judgment. The historical caguitta and the alternative marker l, are retained; ca- continues as caguiri below.

runs.text: Couſa que muito ſe eſtranha, & he

lines.note: Completes satano caguiri and begins the definition of something regarded as astonishingly improper. This row continues both the Japanese phrase and its gloss.

The first explanation concludes with very badly done. Item then introduces another sense of Sata; the repeated term is a sense label rather than a word embedded syntactically in the Portuguese sentence.

runs.text: tica, ou exame ſobre algũa demanda. ¶

lines.note: Completes Pra-tica and describes examining a lawsuit. Removed the OCR's false internal break in exame; Satanin is the following Japanese subentry for the person conducting such proceedings.

runs.text: Iuiz, ou homem q̃ ouue as partes nas deman-

lines.note: Satanin is a judge or someone who hears the parties to a dispute. The q with an abbreviation stroke is kept as q̃; deman- continues on the final body row.
Completes deman-das, lawsuits, and closes the body text. The separate lower-right Sataguai catchword is page furniture and is not merged into this row.

zones.label: Catchword
zones.note: The worn middle g has been read with the visible descending trace and the next page's opening headword. The final mark is a period, not a hyphen.
